title: Triangles
prerequisites: Angle sum property of a triangle.
Properties of parallel lines and a transversal.
Idea of congruent figures as identical in shape and size.
Familiarity with the terms median, altitude and bisector.

topics.title: Congruence of Triangles
topics.quick_summary: Two triangles are congruent if they have exactly the same shape and size, and this can be established by the SSS, SAS, ASA, AAS or RHS criteria.
topics.real_life: Mass-produced roof trusses must be congruent so that any one fits any position — manufacturers verify this by checking three measurements, not six.

detailed.definition: Two triangles are congruent if their corresponding sides and corresponding angles are equal. The congruence criteria are shortcuts that establish this from only three pieces of information.
detailed.key_idea: SAS requires the angle to be between the two sides. SSA is not a valid criterion — two different triangles can share two sides and a non-included angle, which is why it is excluded.
detailed.working_principle: Write the correspondence in the correct order: ΔABC ≅ ΔPQR means A↔P, B↔Q, C↔R. All conclusions about corresponding parts (CPCT) depend on getting this order right.
applications: RHS applies only to right triangles, using the hypotenuse and one side.
AAA is not a congruence criterion — it gives similarity, not congruence.
CPCT is used after proving congruence to deduce equality of remaining parts.

points: Congruence criteria: SSS, SAS, ASA, AAS and RHS.
SAS requires the INCLUDED angle between the two sides.
SSA and AAA are NOT congruence criteria.
Write the correspondence in the correct order when stating congruence.
CPCT — Corresponding Parts of Congruent Triangles are equal — is used after congruence is proved.
mistakes: Using SSA as a congruence criterion.
Writing the vertices in the wrong order in a congruence statement.
Applying AAA and concluding congruence rather than similarity.
topics.memory_hook: 'SSS, SAS, ASA, AAS, RHS' — five valid keys; SSA and AAA open nothing.
topics.advanced: SSA fails because a circle of given radius can cut a line in two places, giving the ambiguous case. In trigonometry this reappears as the two possible solutions of the sine rule.

topics.title: Properties of Triangles and Inequalities
topics.quick_summary: Angles opposite equal sides are equal, the larger angle lies opposite the larger side, and any two sides together exceed the third.
topics.real_life: You cannot build a triangle from sticks of 2 cm, 3 cm and 8 cm — the two shorter sticks simply will not reach across.

detailed.definition: The triangle inequality states that the sum of the lengths of any two sides of a triangle is greater than the third side. In an isosceles triangle, the angles opposite the equal sides are equal.
detailed.key_idea: Side–angle relationships always run in the same direction: bigger side, bigger opposite angle. This one principle covers both the isosceles theorem and the inequality theorems.
detailed.working_principle: To test whether three lengths can form a triangle, it is enough to check that the two smaller lengths together exceed the largest. The other two inequalities then follow automatically.
applications: Angles opposite equal sides are equal, and conversely.
The side opposite the greater angle is longer.
The difference of any two sides is less than the third side.

points: Isosceles triangle: angles opposite the equal sides are equal (and conversely).
The greater side has the greater angle opposite it.
Sum of any two sides > the third side.
Difference of any two sides < the third side.
The perpendicular from a point to a line is the shortest distance to that line.
mistakes: Checking only one of the three triangle inequalities when a length is large.
Reversing the side–angle relation and pairing the largest side with the smallest angle.
Assuming an isosceles triangle must also be acute-angled.
topics.memory_hook: 'Bigger side, bigger angle' — and 'the two short ones must out-reach the long one'.
topics.advanced: The triangle inequality generalises far beyond geometry: it is one of the defining axioms of a metric space, and holds for distances in any dimension, for absolute values, and for vector magnitudes.
